intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. Each note explains a slide, tells you what to remember and warns you where people slip. Work the exercises with a pencil, answer the recall questions without looking, and write your own notes in the margins beside mine.

sections.title: Why design decides outcomes
sections.big_idea: A design is **a written argument** that these activities, here, by this organisation, will change something specific for specific people.
in_plain_words: Programme design is the set of decisions made before money moves: which problem, for whom, through what activities, delivered by whom, at what cost, with what risks, and how the team will learn. A field team can work around a weak plan for a while. It cannot fix a plan aimed at the wrong problem or the wrong people.

Five linked decisions form the cycle: problem, options, choice, plan and learn. Each constrains the next, and looping back when costing fails is a sign the process works. Keep the design, which states reasons, apart from the work plan, which states tasks. **Write the reasons first and the Gantt chart afterwards.**

nodes.label: Problem
nodes.sub: what is wrong, for whom, why

key_terms.meaning: Moving from an analysed problem to a costed, staffed, monitored plan.
Answers why: problem, people, intervention, partner and cost.
Answers when and who; derived from the design.
Invented to teach a method; never a real figure.
The obstacle that most limits an outcome.

worked_example.title: Same goal, different results
worked_example.setup: Two programmes targeted poor households' livelihoods. The Hyderabad microcredit trial found 6.8 new businesses per 100 households against 5.3 in comparison areas.
steps: Business gain: 6.8 − 5.3 = 1.5 more new businesses per 100 households.
The same trial found no significant rise in consumption after 15 to 18 months.
Graduation in Bangladesh transferred livestock and skills to the poorest women, and earnings and assets rose and lasted.
Graduation addressed several constraints together for a tightly targeted group.
Conclude that design choices separated the results.
worked_example.answer: Credit gave 1.5 extra businesses per 100 households and no consumption gain, while the bundled design produced lasting gains.

mistakes: Funding a detailed work plan with a thin design, so reviewers cannot test any argument.
Letting one actor design alone and inherit its blind spots.
Treating costing that sends you back to the delivery model as a failure of process.
Leaving community members out because they have no seat at the table.

recall.q: What does a design document answer, and what does a work plan answer?
recall.a: The design answers why; the work plan answers when and who.

recall.q: What are the five boxes of the design cycle?
recall.a: Problem, options, choice, plan and learn.

recall.q: Why did PM-JAY's targeting choice matter from day one?
recall.a: It used SECC 2011 to identify about 10.74 crore families, which shaped who was covered.

recall.q: What do donors and CSR funders often miss?
recall.a: Local politics and seasonal and caste dynamics.

sections.title: Problem analysis
sections.big_idea: Define **the problem without naming a solution**, build causes below it, check each arrow against data and choose which branches you act on.
in_plain_words: A problem statement describes a negative condition, who is affected, how large it is and where, and it never names your intervention. A problem tree puts direct causes below and effects above, and root-cause analysis keeps asking why until you reach something a programme can act on. TaRL began with such a diagnosis: children were enrolled but taught at grade level.

A tree is a hypothesis until data supports it, and the people affected should help define the problem. Size it and locate it, because a national average hides concentration. Then turn causes into objectives and say which you leave to others. **No programme addresses every cause.**

key_terms.meaning: A negative condition, who, how large and where, without a solution.
Causes below a focal problem, effects above.
The problem tree rewritten as positive achievements.
A cause the programme can influence.
The year and survey round behind a figure.

worked_example.title: Rewrite and size a problem
worked_example.setup: A draft says 'Lack of a mobile app'. NFHS-5 gives stunting at 35.5% for India.
steps: The draft names a missing solution, so it fails the test.
Rewrite it: 'Half of Class 5 children in the block cannot read a Class 2 text.'
Size by place: Meghalaya 46.5% against the India 35.5% is 46.5 − 35.5 = 11.0 points above.
Kerala at 23.4% is 35.5 − 23.4 = 12.1 points below the India figure.
Note the vintage: NFHS-5 for states and 29.3% in NFHS-6 for India.
worked_example.answer: A problem statement without a solution, and a state spread of 11.0 points above and 12.1 below the NFHS-5 average.

mistakes: Starting from a favourite intervention and writing the problem to fit.
Using a state average to justify a district programme.
Using data more than a decade old as if current.
Treating a problem as uniform when causes differ, for example between tribal and non-tribal blocks.

recall.q: What is the test for a problem statement?
recall.a: If it contains the name of your intervention, rewrite it.

recall.q: How do you turn a problem tree into an objectives tree?
recall.a: Rewrite each negative situation as a positive achievement.

recall.q: What did the Janani Suraksha Yojana evidence say about supply?
recall.a: Cash raised facility births but quality of obstetric care needed attention.

recall.q: Why record causes left to others?
recall.a: It makes the programme's boundary visible, and each becomes an assumption to monitor.

sections.title: Stakeholders and power
sections.big_idea: Map everyone who affects or is affected by the programme, **including those who lose**, and note that power in a village is often informal.
in_plain_words: A stakeholder analysis assesses each party's interest, influence and likely response. The power-interest grid sorts them into four boxes, but it is a starting point, because caste, land, kinship and party hold power that no organogram shows. A political economy analysis asks who gains, who loses and who decides.

Design for the people who deliver, since the last mile runs through a few frontline workers who already carry many logs. Plan participation by decision, and seek out people at the edges, such as Dalit and Adivasi hamlets. **Record who was consulted and what changed as a result.**

key_terms.meaning: A structured assessment of interest, influence and response.
How power, incentives and institutions shape what can work.
A person at the last mile, such as an ASHA or teacher.
Charting a worker's week before adding tasks.
Local elites taking the benefit of a programme.

worked_example.title: Place stakeholders on the grid
worked_example.setup: Use the slide's examples to place six stakeholders.
steps: District collector, state mission director and funder: high power, high interest, so manage closely.
Intended participants and frontline workers: low power, high interest, so keep informed and give voice.
A finance department or a busy block development officer: high power, low interest, so keep satisfied.
Moneylenders affected by a credit scheme: monitor, and expect them to act even if not invited.
worked_example.answer: Manage closely, keep informed and give voice, keep satisfied, monitor.

mistakes: Leaving out people who lose from the programme.
Reading the Udaipur result as a monitoring failure only. The enforcers' incentives were never in the design.
Piling a new app, log and survey on frontline workers without paying for the added work.
Calling meetings only through the sarpanch, which reproduces the village hierarchy.

recall.q: What happened in the Udaipur nurse programme?
recall.a: Attendance rose at first, then within about 16 months the difference disappeared as the local administration undermined the incentives.

recall.q: Name two questions a political economy analysis asks.
recall.a: Who controls the resource, and which officials must act and what are they rewarded for.

recall.q: What size are Kudumbashree neighbourhood groups?
recall.a: 10 to 20 women, one member per family.

recall.q: How should you hold meetings with marginal groups?
recall.a: Separately, and record what they say separately.

sections.title: Evidence before design
sections.big_idea: Find out what has been tried, weigh each type of evidence for the question it answers, and **write down the mechanism** before you copy anything.
in_plain_words: An evidence review stops you repeating failed designs and shows when others worked. Systematic reviews give an average, randomised trials give a causal effect in one setting, process evaluations show how delivery worked, and monitoring data show reach and cost. A design needs both causal and operational evidence.

Whether a study transfers depends on the mechanism. Bihar's bicycles cut the time and safety cost of reaching school, which matters most where schools are far. Copying features without the mechanism is isomorphic mimicry. Null results are valuable, and where evidence is thin you pilot and set decision rules. **Admitting uncertainty makes a design stronger.**

key_terms.meaning: The reason an intervention produces its effect.
Copying the form of a model without its function.
The parts that carry the mechanism.
An evaluation that found no effect.
Reports outside journals, such as audits and evaluations.

worked_example.title: Will the bicycle programme transfer?
worked_example.setup: Bihar's programme raised girls' age-appropriate enrolment by 32 per cent and cut the gender gap by 40 per cent, mostly where villages were farther from a secondary school.
steps: State the mechanism: the bicycle reduced the time and safety cost of the journey.
District A has secondary schools far from villages and cycle-friendly roads: likely to transfer.
District B has a secondary school in every village: unlikely to transfer.
District C's constraint is early marriage or fees: unlikely to transfer.
Check that the reason holds in your setting before copying.
worked_example.answer: It transfers to District A only, because the mechanism is travel cost.

mistakes: Searching only for success stories and skipping nulls such as Hyderabad microcredit.
Taking a randomised result from one setting as proof it will work in yours.
Removing components of a package such as graduation without testing the smaller version.
Claiming certainty where evidence is thin instead of planning a pilot.

recall.q: What does a process evaluation tell you and not tell you?
recall.a: How and why delivery worked or broke, with no estimate of impact.

recall.q: What are three questions to ask of a null result?
recall.a: Was it delivered as designed, was the sample large enough, and was the right outcome measured.

recall.q: What does the TaRL mechanism consist of?
recall.a: Grouping by learning level with simple, frequent assessment.

recall.q: What are the four steps when evidence is thin?
recall.a: State what is known, name the weakest assumptions, pilot those first, and set decision rules.

sections.title: Choosing the intervention and delivery model
sections.big_idea: Compare **at least three options** on the same criteria, match the channel to the mechanism, and protect the dosage the mechanism needs.
in_plain_words: Generate several options, including doing less, using an existing scheme and a cash alternative. Score them on evidence, cost per outcome, feasibility, scalability, equity and risk, with the people who will deliver. The cash benchmark does not always win, but it forces you to say what in-kind or service delivery adds.

Match the channel to the mechanism, whether trust through community workers, uniform transfers through digital payment, or mentoring through the education department. Set dosage by what the mechanism needs, keep the core, and adapt the periphery. **Check every choice for gendered effects.**

key_terms.meaning: Asking whether cash to participants would do more good.
Who delivers and through what channel.
The quantity of intervention a participant receives.
The component that carries the mechanism.
Language, timing and host institution, which can adapt.

worked_example.title: Work out a TaRL dose
worked_example.setup: J-PAL describes TaRL camps of ten days at two to three hours a day, with three to five camps a year.
steps: Hours in one camp, low end: 10 × 2 = 20 hours.
Hours in one camp, high end: 10 × 3 = 30 hours.
Days a year with three camps: 3 × 10 = 30 days.
Days a year with five camps: 5 × 10 = 50 days.
Cutting the dose to fit a budget changes the intervention.
worked_example.answer: 20 to 30 hours a camp and 30 to 50 days a year.

mistakes: Considering one option, which teams tend to fund.
Scoring options alone as the proposal writer, which is a justification exercise.
Setting dosage from budget arithmetic when it should follow the mechanism.
Paying a transfer into the household head's account without asking who controls it.

recall.q: Name three options a team should list.
recall.a: Doing less, working through an existing scheme and a cash alternative.

recall.q: Which delivery model fits the mechanism of rapid, uniform transfer of money?
recall.a: A digital payment system.

recall.q: What is the rule if the budget cannot pay for an effective dose for everyone?
recall.a: Reach fewer people properly before reaching more thinly.

recall.q: What is the advice about the pilot's delivery model?
recall.a: Design the model you would use at scale, then pilot that.

sections.title: Targeting
sections.big_idea: Every targeting rule makes **two kinds of mistake**. Design chooses which to accept, and exclusion is usually the larger harm.
in_plain_words: Targeting is needed when the budget cannot cover everyone or the intervention helps only some. Methods include categorical, geographic, proxy means tests, census deprivation lists, community ranking and self-targeting, and most large programmes combine them. Pakistan's scorecard and the Indonesian field experiment show the trade-offs between formulas and communities.

Lists age. PM-JAY's list was seven years old at launch. Even eligible people can miss out because of documents, bank links, biometrics or travel. Before you finalise, answer the seven questions in the checklist, and remember that **universal coverage in a small area can be cheaper and fairer**.

left.title: Exclusion error
items: An eligible person is left out
Often the poorest and least connected
Usually the larger harm to participants

key_terms.meaning: A score from observable assets that predicts consumption.
Everyone in a group is eligible, such as older people.
Everyone in selected areas is eligible.
A benefit designed so only the needy apply.
A list of households that other programmes can reuse.

worked_example.title: Pick a method and test the list
worked_example.setup: Choose a targeting method for three programmes and check a list's age.
steps: An old-age pension: categorical, since everyone in the group is eligible.
A district-wide school programme: geographic, as in the Aspirational Districts Programme.
A national health scheme using SECC 2011: a census deprivation list.
The list's age at the 2018 launch: 2018 − 2011 = 7 years.
Add a continuous enrolment window and verification at the gram panchayat for new applicants.
worked_example.answer: Categorical, geographic and census list; the list was seven years old at launch.

mistakes: Counting only inclusion errors because they look like leakage.
Treating a registry as finished without a plan and budget for updating it.
Using community ranking where caste or gender hierarchies are strong, with no safeguards.
Assuming eligibility means receipt, when documents and biometrics stand in the way.

recall.q: What did the Indonesian experiment find about community targeting?
recall.a: It did somewhat worse than a proxy means test against consumption, but communities were more satisfied.

recall.q: What are weaknesses of a proxy means test?
recall.a: Large errors near the threshold, an ageing registry and households unable to see why they were excluded.

recall.q: Give two design responses to documentation barriers.
recall.a: Accept alternative documents, and camp-based enrolment or doorstep service.

recall.q: What question explains who your programme will miss when you design within a scheme?
recall.a: How its list was built and when.

sections.title: Theory of change, budget and cost per outcome
sections.big_idea: The theory of change and the budget are **two parts of one argument**. Cost per outcome is what lets you compare designs.
in_plain_words: A theory of change is the causal chain from inputs to impact, with an assumption between every pair of boxes. Designs fail more often at the arrows than in the boxes, so list each assumption, rate the evidence and rate the damage if it is false. Focus monitoring and the pilot on high-damage, weak-evidence assumptions.

A budget is built bottom up from activities and must include the often-missed lines: participants' costs, incentives, translation, grievance handling and retraining. Compute cost per outcome, cost at scale and cost at government norms. Know the legal limits, such as FCRA s7 and the 20 per cent cap. **Pay for results only where outcomes can be measured credibly.**

diagram.caption: an assumption sits at every arrow

key_terms.meaning: A condition that must hold between two steps of the chain.
Built from activities, quantities and unit costs.
Cost divided by what the programme changes.
A fixed rate in scheme guidelines or state orders.
A contract where an outcome funder repays an investor for results.

worked_example.title: Cost per additional reader
worked_example.setup: Illustrative options: A camps cost ₹1,200 per child for a 20 percentage point gain. B textbooks cost ₹400 for 2 points. C teacher training costs ₹800 for 5 points.
steps: Option A: 1,200 ÷ 0.20 = 6,000 rupees per additional reader.
Option B: 400 ÷ 0.02 = 20,000 rupees.
Option C: 800 ÷ 0.05 = 16,000 rupees.
Rank by cost per reader: A, then C, then B.
Check a government norm gap: mentor pay of ₹25,000 against ₹18,000 is 25,000 − 18,000 = 7,000 a month.
worked_example.answer: A costs ₹6,000 per reader, C ₹16,000 and B ₹20,000. The cheapest per child is the dearest per reader.

mistakes: Comparing options on cost per output or cost per child.
Costing the pilot at the NGO's own prices, so the results describe a programme the state cannot buy.
Using a pilot's cost per participant as the cost at scale.
Passing foreign contributions on as a sub-grant, which FCRA s7 prohibits.

recall.q: What does a good theory of change let you see at each arrow?
recall.a: What would have to be true and how you would know if it was not.

recall.q: Which assumptions should monitoring and the pilot focus on first?
recall.a: High-damage, weak-evidence assumptions.

recall.q: What cap does FCRA s8(1)(b) place on administrative expenses?
recall.a: 20 per cent in a financial year unless the Central Government approves more.

recall.q: Why does cost per participant change with scale?
recall.a: Fixed costs spread over more people, but supervision layers and harder areas can raise it again.

sections.title: Risk and safeguarding at design stage
sections.big_idea: List risks, assess harms and **build safeguarding, data protection and a complaint route into the design**, with budget lines and named owners.
in_plain_words: A risk log rates each risk for likelihood and impact, chooses a response and names an owner. Severe-impact risks need a response even when unlikely. Do-no-harm thinking asks, for each activity, who could be harmed, how and what prevents it. Staff, volunteers and lenders have power over participants.

Indian law adds duties: POCSO s19 and s21 on reporting, the 2013 Act on workplace committees, and the DPDP rules from 13 May 2027. Design a grievance route that is free, local, safe and answered in time. **A programme with no complaints usually has an inaccessible mechanism.**

diagram.caption: the four responses in the deck

key_terms.meaning: A reviewed list of risks with likelihood, impact, response, owner.
Assessing how an activity could hurt participants.
Preventing sexual exploitation and abuse.
A duty to report offences against children.
A route to complain and get a timed answer.

worked_example.title: Rate risks and respond
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's illustrative log to choose responses.
steps: Staff abuse of a child: low likelihood, severe impact, so vetting, two-adult rule and POCSO training.
Government funds released late: high likelihood, medium impact, so a bridge fund.
Elite capture of selection: medium likelihood, high impact, so public reading of lists and an appeal route.
Extreme heat: high likelihood, medium impact, so shift to mornings with shade and water.
Name an owner for each, such as the safeguarding lead.
worked_example.answer: A response and an owner for every risk, with severe risks covered even when unlikely.

mistakes: Leaving safeguarding without a budget line.
Collecting caste, religion or health data without a lawful basis, notice and security.
Treating reporting under POCSO as an institutional duty only. It is a personal legal duty.
Building the grievance route after a scandal.

recall.q: What does section 21 of POCSO do?
recall.a: It makes failure to report punishable, with a longer term for a person in charge of an institution.

recall.q: What does the 2013 workplace Act require of an employer?
recall.a: An Internal Committee under section 4.

recall.q: When do the DPDP duties apply?
recall.a: From 13 May 2027.

recall.q: Name the five steps of the grievance process.
recall.a: Receive, record, resolve, respond and review.

sections.title: Implementation planning and adaptive management
sections.big_idea: Plan phases, supervision and **decision rules agreed in advance**, so monitoring turns into decisions and the plan can change.
in_plain_words: An implementation plan sets phases, staffing, procurement, a calendar, a monitoring plan and decision points. The South Asian calendar includes seasons, school terms, festivals, the April to March financial year and the model code of conduct. Fidelity falls as supervision thins, so plan ratios and turnover.

A pilot tests delivery and the riskiest assumptions under conditions close to scale, with rules agreed first. Monitoring should serve decisions. Adaptive management builds learning cycles and permission to change into the plan, and the grant should allow it. **Plan the exit at the start.**

diagram.caption: phasing with a decision point built in

key_terms.meaning: How far delivery matches the design.
A test of whether the design can be delivered at scale conditions.
Adjusting the programme in response to learning within agreed limits.
A threshold agreed in advance that triggers a change.
The share of budget movable between lines without approval.

worked_example.title: Apply decision rules
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: 20 level-based sessions were scheduled in a month and 11 were held. Budgeted cost per child is ₹1,200 and actual cost is ₹1,440.
steps: Sessions held as scheduled: 11 ÷ 20 = 55%.
The rule says below 60% means redesign the timetable with headteachers, so act.
Cost over budget: 1,440 − 1,200 = 240 rupees per child.
Over the budget share: 240 ÷ 1,200 = 20%.
The rule triggers at over 20% above, so 20% sits at the line and needs a close look.
worked_example.answer: Sessions at 55% trigger redesign of the timetable; cost is exactly 20% over, at the edge of the rule.

mistakes: Running the pilot with the best staff and extra funding, which flatters the design.
Deciding after the pilot what counts as success.
Planning one training and assuming no one leaves.
Filling a dashboard with indicators nobody uses for a decision.

recall.q: Why does fidelity fall as programmes grow?
recall.a: Supervision gets thinner.

recall.q: What should a useful pilot have?
recall.a: Written questions, decision rules agreed in advance, assumption monitoring, cost data and a review date.

recall.q: What is Problem-Driven Iterative Adaptation?
recall.a: An approach solving locally nominated problems with experimentation, rapid feedback loops and many agents.

recall.q: Name the four exit routes.
recall.a: Government takes over, a community institution continues, time-limited by design, or a market continues.

sections.title: Government partnership and design for scale
sections.big_idea: Most programmes reach scale through the state. **Design with government from the start**, pilot through the scaling implementer and expect effects to shrink.
in_plain_words: State systems run schools, health and social protection for most poor households, so an NGO programme matters mainly if it changes what those systems do. Work within schemes and know their features, as the rural employment scheme shows. Choose a partnership model and write an MoU. JEEViKA grew from a state project into a national mission.

Distinguish horizontal scaling from vertical scaling and use the CORRECT checklist. Effects shrink at scale because implementers, populations and politics change. Evaluate inside government systems, with ethics review. **Aim to change a scheme's design or delivery** more than to run a parallel programme.

left.title: Horizontal scaling
items: A cost the system can afford

right.title: Vertical scaling
items: Changes in guidelines or budget heads

key_terms.meaning: Expansion and replication to new places and people.
Institutionalisation through policy, budgets and law.
A memorandum of understanding setting roles and exit.
The shrinking of effects as programmes scale.
A per-state funding amount, with excess spending borne by the state.

worked_example.title: JEEViKA's expansion
worked_example.setup: JEEViKA began in 42 blocks of six high-poverty districts and expanded in phases to 102 blocks in the same districts.
steps: New blocks added: 102 − 42 = 60.
It saturated its first blocks before moving on.
It was run by an autonomous society loged for the purpose.
The 2017 completion report records that the national mission was designed largely on its model.
Open questions remain on federation quality at national scale.
worked_example.answer: Sixty blocks were added in phases, and the model informed the national mission.

mistakes: Designing a parallel programme with its own workers and logs, then hoping for adoption.
Piloting through the best implementer while planning to scale through a weaker one.
Treating effects from a pilot as guaranteed at scale.
Ignoring the 60-day seasonal pause when scheduling complementary activities.

recall.q: What does the CORRECT checklist cover?
recall.a: Credible, observable, relevant, relative advantage, easy to install, compatible and testable.

recall.q: What did the Kenyan contract-teacher study show?
recall.a: NGO-hired teachers raised test scores and government-hired teachers on identical contracts produced no effect.

recall.q: Name three partnership models.
recall.a: Any three of technical support, embedded implementation, government adoption, contracted delivery and joint evaluation.

recall.q: What does experimentation at scale answer?
recall.a: What happens if the state itself does this, across whole districts, with its own staff and budgets.

sections.title: Practical application
sections.big_idea: The worked example shows each decision **written with its reason**, so a funder can see what was left out and why.
in_plain_words: An NGO is asked to design a three-year reading programme in eastern Uttar Pradesh. The problem is that most Class 3 to 5 children in four blocks cannot read a Class 2 text, and vacancies are noted as an assumption outside scope. The team compares camps, a government teacher model and books, and picks the model the department can continue.

Targeting is geographic, the budget is bottom up with a safeguarding line, and risks are paired with responses. The plan has a decision point at the end of year one with rules agreed in advance. Use the two checklists and the appraisal questions on your own work. **A design that ticks every item can still fail.**

key_terms.meaning: A cause left to others and recorded as an assumption.
How well an option suits later adoption by government.
All government primary schools in four blocks.
A date when agreed rules decide continue, adapt or stop.
Reviewing someone else's design with a set of questions.

worked_example.title: Check an expansion rule
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: in year one, 600 children are assessed each term and 72 move up a reading level. The rule says below 15% means review teaching practice before expansion.
steps: Share moving up: 72 ÷ 600 = 12%.
Compare with the threshold: 12% is below 15%.
The rule says review teaching practice before expansion.
So expansion to the other blocks waits.
Without the rule every result would be read as a reason to continue.
worked_example.answer: 12% is under the 15% line, so expansion waits until teaching practice is reviewed.

mistakes: Choosing the delivery model by evidence only, with no regard to what the department can continue.
Targeting through household lists when school-based targeting avoids document exclusion.
Skipping the risk of volunteers having contact with children during assessments.
Reading every result as success because no rules were agreed.

recall.q: Why was option B, the government teacher model, chosen?
recall.a: The funder and district wanted a model the department could continue after three years.

recall.q: Which cause is out of scope in the example?
recall.a: Teacher vacancies, which belong to the state department and are noted as an assumption.

recall.q: What rule applies if mentor visits fall below one a month?
recall.a: Renegotiate mentor time with the district.

recall.q: What do funders and CSR committees do with the appraisal questions?
recall.a: They use them directly and ask for written answers.

sections.title: Common design failures
sections.big_idea: Seven failures recur, and **most are visible in the design document** if someone asks the right question before the grant is signed.
in_plain_words: Solution first, wrong cause, ignored incentives, thin dosage, pilot-only conditions, exclusion by design and no learning loop. Each has a prevention in the table. The Udaipur case shows enforcers opting out, and Hyderabad microcredit shows over-promising against the mechanism.

Parallel systems also fail, since they leave nothing behind when funding ends. A pre-mortem catches doubts early: imagine the programme has failed, write reasons independently, pool them and check each against the log, assumptions, monitoring and budget. **Return to the section behind each principle** when a review raises a question.

key_terms.meaning: Imagining failure first to surface doubts.
A project building its own systems beside the state.
Claiming more than the mechanism can deliver.
Enforcers or staff undermine a design that never considered them.
Monitoring and decision rules that surface problems early.

worked_example.title: Spot a parallel programme
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a project pays mentors ₹25,000 a month against a government norm of ₹18,000, and runs its own data system.
steps: Pay compared with the norm: 25,000 ÷ 18,000 = 1.39 times.
Pay above government scales is a warning sign.
A separate data system with no link to government MIS is another.
The alternative is to work through government staff and cost at government norms.
Agree a handover timeline with the department from the start.
worked_example.answer: Mentor pay is 1.39 times the norm and the data system is separate, so the project is a parallel programme.

mistakes: Relying on a local administration to penalise its own staff without checking enforcement.
Promising poverty reduction through credit alone, then counting repayment as success.
Ending a funded project with an exit plan that says only 'advocacy for adoption'.
Brainstorming risks in a meeting where senior voices set the agenda.

recall.q: What should you ask of every rule in a design?
recall.a: Who enforces it, and what do they gain or lose by doing so?

recall.q: What did attendance do in the Udaipur programme in its first months?
recall.a: It rose by 15 to 29 percentage points according to J-PAL.

recall.q: How long should a pre-mortem take, and how are reasons gathered?
recall.a: Ninety minutes, with reasons written independently before discussion.

recall.q: Name two warning signs of a parallel programme.
recall.a: Project staff paid far above government scales, and data systems with no link to government MIS.

notes.2: Use the agenda to see the order of decisions: problem, people, evidence, intervention, targeting, theory of change and budget, risk, implementation, government and scale. Section 11 puts them together in a worked case and section 12 lists how designs fail. **Read in order the first time**, because each section constrains the next.
notes.4: Hold on to the sentence that a design is a written argument. It claims that a particular bundle of activities, in a particular place, by a particular organisation, will change something specific for specific people. The slide's blunt point is that **a field team cannot fix a plan aimed at the wrong problem**.
notes.5: Read the cycle as five linked decisions, each constraining the next: problem, options, choice, plan, learn. The slide's last paragraph is useful: when costing shows the plan is unaffordable and sends you back to the delivery model, **the process is working**. Expect to loop.
notes.6: Compare the two programmes, which both aimed at poor households' livelihoods. The Hyderabad microcredit trial found more new businesses and no significant rise in consumption, while graduation in Bangladesh raised earnings and assets for years. The difference was design: **several binding constraints for a tightly targeted group** against one lever for many.
notes.7: Design choices move large budgets. PM-JAY set out to cover about 10.74 crore families identified from SECC 2011, and that targeting choice shaped who was covered from day one. Take the closing line as your warning: **an old list, a narrow definition or a costly channel** is carried into every year.
notes.8: Read each row for a strength and a blind spot. NGOs know the field and miss costing at scale. Funders bring money and miss local politics. Government brings mandate and misses permission to fail. Researchers bring evidence and miss operations. **Community members usually lack a seat at all.** Bring all five in without making a committee document.
notes.9: Keep the design document and the work plan apart. The design answers why, names its assumptions and says how each will be checked. The work plan answers when and who, and changes often. A work plan with no design behind it gives you activity reports and no learning. **Write the reasons first and the Gantt chart afterwards.**
notes.10: Use the roadmap to place yourself. Sections 2 to 6 run from problem to targeting, section 7 joins theory of change with budget, sections 8 to 10 cover risk, delivery and government, and 11 and 12 apply and warn. Note the convention: anything labelled **Illustrative is invented to teach a method**, while named programmes are real and sourced.
notes.12: The commonest design error is starting with a solution and writing the problem to fit. A problem statement describes a negative condition, who is affected, its scale and its place, with no intervention in it. Run the slide's test: **if your statement contains your intervention's name, rewrite it.**
notes.13: Build the problem tree with causes below and effects above, in a participatory workshop. Keep asking what causes each cause. Then flip each negative into a positive to get the objectives tree. The tree on the slide is illustrative, so **a real tree needs teachers, parents and children** and a check against data.
notes.14: Keep asking why until you reach a cause the programme can act on. The TaRL case shows the pay-off: children were enrolled but taught at grade level while years behind, so the fix was grouping by learning level. Follow the four boxes from low reading levels to **'act here'**.
notes.15: Treat every problem tree as a hypothesis. Each causal arrow should be checked against data such as NFHS, ASER, PLFS, the Census or scheme records. Use the three rows as templates: claim, evidence that would support it, where to look. Where no data exists, **a short diagnostic study is cheaper** than a programme built on a wrong cause.
notes.16: Compare an outsider's definition with the insider's. A funder sees low institutional delivery and designs for demand, while women describe being shouted at and sent onward at night. The JSY evidence shows cash raised facility births and was linked to fewer perinatal deaths, yet quality of care stayed unreached. **Let affected people define the problem first.**
notes.17: Size the problem and find where it concentrates. NFHS-5 stunting is 35.5% nationally and ranges from 46.5% in Meghalaya to 23.4% in Kerala. Compare state figures with the NFHS-5 India figure, since NFHS-6 gives 29.3%. **Note the vintage of every figure** and recheck when new data arrive.
notes.18: Turn causes into objectives and then choose. No programme tackles every cause, so the table has a column for who acts on each. Putting 'state education department (out of scope)' beside teacher vacancies makes the boundary visible. That row becomes **an assumption to monitor** in the theory of change.
notes.20: List everyone who can affect or is affected by the programme: participants and those excluded, frontline workers, officials, traders, moneylenders, community leaders, other NGOs and the funder. Include the people who lose, such as moneylenders or officials who gain from opacity. **They will act even if they are not invited.**
notes.21: Place each stakeholder in one of four boxes: manage closely, keep informed, keep satisfied, monitor. Low-power participants and frontline workers need channels made for them. The grid is only a start, because **power in a village is often informal** and absent from any organogram.
notes.22: The Udaipur nurse study is the standard warning. Time-stamping machines and pay deductions raised attendance, and within about 16 months the difference had disappeared because the local health administration undermined the incentives. The design worked on paper and failed in the hands of those who had to enforce it. **Their incentives were never in the design.**
notes.23: Use these five questions as a short political economy note. Who controls the resource, which officials must act and what are they rewarded for, which elites benefit, what happens at transfer or election, and what norms shape access? Keep the note internal where it names people, because **a published version usually says nothing**.
notes.24: Design for the people who deliver it. Frontline workers carry most last-mile delivery, and each new programme tends to add a log, an app or a meeting. Compare the two lists on the slide: overload versus fit. A **time-use map of a worker's week** before design is cheap and often decisive.
notes.25: Be specific about which decisions participants will influence, because participation ranges from a consultation after decisions to shared control of budgets. Kudumbashree's neighbourhood groups of 10 to 20 women, now 2,57,627 of them, show a structure built on participation. Participation costs time and wages, so **budget for it**.
notes.26: Stakeholder maps drawn from the village centre miss people at the edges. Meetings called through the sarpanch tend to reproduce the existing hierarchy. Walk every hamlet, hold separate meetings and ask a disability organisation to review. Then **record who was consulted and what changed**, so a funder can check whether inclusion shaped decisions.
notes.28: Before designing, find out what has been tried. An evidence review prevents repeating failed designs and shows the conditions under which others worked. Search the 3ie portal, Campbell and Cochrane, J-PAL and IPA, and the South Asian grey literature. The pointer to Systematic Reviews 101 covers **how to search and appraise properly**.
notes.29: Use the table to match evidence to the question. A review gives an average effect, a randomised trial a causal effect in one setting, a process evaluation shows how delivery worked, and monitoring data show reach and cost. A design needs **both causal and operational evidence**, because neither covers the other.
notes.30: The bicycle evidence shows transfer depends on mechanism. Bihar's programme cut the time and safety cost of getting to school, and gains were largest in villages farther from a secondary school. Write down why the intervention worked, then **check whether that reason holds in your district**.
notes.31: A mechanism is the reason an intervention works. TaRL works because instruction matches the child's level, bicycles because they cut the cost of the journey, graduation because several constraints ease together. Copying visible features without the mechanism is isomorphic mimicry. **Separate the core that carries the mechanism from the adaptable periphery.**
notes.32: Work through the graduation review as a template: identify the studies, state each finding, then draw the design implication. Impacts lasted at least a year after support ended and gains persisted for four and seven years. Notice the third row: **removing components needs its own test**, because the package works as a bundle.
notes.33: Search for evidence that something did not work, as well as success stories. The Hyderabad microcredit trial found no significant rise in consumption. When you read a null, ask whether delivery matched the design, whether the sample could detect a plausible effect, and whether the right outcome was measured. **Record nulls in the design document.**
notes.34: When no rigorous study exists, say so plainly and design to learn. The four steps run from stating what is known to setting decision rules: continue, adapt or stop. The slide ends with a judgement you can use with funders: **a design that admits uncertainty and plans to resolve it is stronger.**
notes.36: Generate at least three distinct options, including doing less, using an existing scheme and a cash alternative, then compare them on the same six criteria. The familiar option is often neither cheapest nor likeliest to work. Score with the people who will deliver, because **a score done by the proposal writer alone is a justification exercise**.
notes.37: Ask whether the programme does more good than handing the budget over as cash. The cash benchmark does not always win; it forces you to state what an in-kind or service programme adds. Cash fits when needs differ and markets work. In-kind fits when there is a **coordination or safety problem**, such as girls cycling together.
notes.38: Read the table as a menu of channels, each with a strength and a weakness. Government systems have reach and permanence but overloaded staff. Community institutions bring ownership and risk capture by the better-off. Digital channels are fast and **exclude the unconnected**. Pick the channel with its weakness in mind.
notes.39: Match the delivery model to the mechanism. Trust and repeated contact suggest a community worker, rapid uniform transfer suggests digital payment, and changing classroom practice has to go through the education department's mentoring. The closing rule: **design the model you would use at scale, then pilot that**.
notes.40: Dosage is how much, how often and for how long. TaRL camps usually run ten days at two to three hours a day, with three to five camps giving 30 to 50 days a year. Cutting dosage to fit a budget changes the intervention. If funds fall short, **reach fewer people properly before reaching more thinly**.
notes.41: Use the two lists as a test when adapting a model. Core components carry the mechanism: minimum dosage, selection rule and feedback loop. The periphery can change: language, timing, host institution. Graduation changed its asset across countries and kept its combination. **If unsure whether a component is core, assume it is.**
notes.42: Check every design choice for gendered effects. Midday training excludes women doing household work, transfers into a household head's account go to men, and livestock adds unpaid work. Bangladesh's stipend paid into girls' own accounts. The table gives four questions to ask: **timing, ownership, staffing and what you count**.
notes.44: Targeting decides who a programme is for, and every rule makes two kinds of mistake. Exclusion error leaves out eligible people, often the poorest. Inclusion error gives benefits to the ineligible, which looks like leakage and is often less harmful. Decide explicitly which you care about more. **Exclusion is usually the larger harm to participants.**
notes.45: Learn the six methods by example: categorical, geographic, proxy means test, census deprivation list, community-based and self-targeting. Each has its own strengths. Most large programmes combine methods in sequence, such as **a geographic filter, then a list, then community verification**.
notes.46: Pakistan's scorecard shows a proxy means test at scale: a door-to-door survey of 27 million households and a threshold on the score. Strengths are a transparent rule and a reusable registry. Weaknesses are errors near the threshold and an ageing registry. **A registry needs a plan and a budget for updating.**
notes.47: The Indonesian field experiment compared a proxy means test, community ranking and a hybrid. Community targeting did somewhat worse against consumption yet satisfied people more, because communities used a different idea of poverty. Where caste or gender hierarchies are strong, add **safeguards such as separate meetings and an appeal route**.
notes.48: Ask how a scheme's list was built and when. PM-JAY's list of about 10.74 crore families came from SECC 2011, seven years old at launch. Households that became poor later or formed afterwards stay excluded until the list is updated. Each fix adds administrative work, so **budget for the staff time** and monitor who uses the route.
notes.49: Eligibility on paper differs from access in practice. Documents, bank accounts, mobile links, biometrics and travel to an office stand between a person and a benefit, and they fall hardest on the marginal. For each step the table gives a design response. **Map every step from eligibility to receipt.**
notes.50: Use the seven questions as a sign-off for targeting. They run from defining the group in one sentence to the cost of targeting per person reached. The closing line is a useful reminder: **universal coverage within a small area can be cheaper and fairer** than precise targeting once identification costs are counted.
notes.52: A theory of change is the causal argument written as a chain: inputs, activities, outputs, outcomes, impact. This deck covers it briefly, and Theory of Change 101 and Logframe 101 go further. At each arrow, ask **what would have to be true and how you would know if it was not**.
notes.53: The assumptions between boxes are where designs fail. List each one, rate the evidence for it and rate the damage if it were false. In the illustrative table, a fortnightly mentor visit has weak evidence, so the action is monthly monitoring. **Focus monitoring and the pilot on high-damage, weak-evidence assumptions.**
notes.54: A budget is part of the argument. Reviewers read it to see if the plan is serious: enough staff for the dosage, funded monitoring and evaluation, participants' costs, a safeguarding line. Build it bottom up from activities, and avoid inflating last year's figures. **Check the list of lines often missing**, such as participants' lost wages.
notes.55: Compute cost per outcome instead of cost per output. In the illustrative table, the cheapest option per child, new textbooks at ₹400, costs ₹20,000 per additional reader, while level-based camps at ₹1,200 cost ₹6,000. 1,200 ÷ 0.20 = 6,000. **Compare options on a range of cost per outcome.**
notes.56: Cost per participant changes with scale. Fixed costs spread over more people, so cost falls, and at very large scale it can rise again for harder-to-reach areas and layered supervision. A pilot's cost per participant is **a poor guide to cost at scale**, in either direction. The chart is illustrative.
notes.57: Cost the model at the prices the system will pay. If a pilot pays mentors twice the government rate, its results describe a programme the state cannot buy. Keep two columns from the start, the NGO pilot cost and the government norm, and a plan for each gap. **Look up actual norms** before costing.
notes.58: An outcome-linked contract pays for results. In the Educate Girls bond an investor supplied US$270,000 upfront, an evaluator measured results and the outcome funder repaid according to them. These contracts need credible measurement and an evaluation budget. They also **push effort toward what is measured**, so choose the metric carefully.
notes.59: Indian law shapes the budget. Under FCRA s7 a foreign-funded NGO cannot pass money on as a sub-grant, and s8(1)(b) caps administrative expenses at 20 per cent. Corporate funding must fall within Schedule VII. Classify lines early, and **check the current text** because rules changed in 2026.
notes.61: Treat risk as a design output. List risks across categories, rate likelihood and impact, and choose a response: avoid, reduce, transfer or accept and monitor. The product is a log owned by a named person and reviewed on a schedule. The illustrative table shows a category for **harm to people**, which many logs skip.
notes.62: Programmes can harm the people they aim to help. Cash may raise violence risk, microfinance groups may pressure repayment, and caste or health data can expose people. For each activity, ask who could be harmed, how, and what prevents it. **Put the harm assessment in the design document, with a budget line.**
notes.63: Section 19 of the POCSO Act makes reporting a personal duty for anyone who knows or apprehends an offence, and section 21 makes failure punishable, with a longer term for a person in charge of an institution. Turn this into design: a written reporting procedure, training for everyone, **a named senior officer** and vetting.
notes.64: PSEA is highest where staff decide who gets something of value. Design can reduce it by removing single points of discretion, publishing criteria and telling participants that the benefit is free and how to report. At the workplace, the 2013 Act requires an Internal Committee. Note that **the Labour Codes also apply** to staff contracts.
notes.65: Programmes collect names, phone numbers, caste and health data. The DPDP Act and Rules impose duties from 13 May 2027, so a programme running past that date should design data collection now. The research exemption helps evaluation and does not cover routine operations. Use the table: **collect only fields someone will use**.
notes.66: Design the complaint route at the start. It should be free, local, in the local language, confidential and answered within a stated time. The five steps run from receiving to reviewing patterns. Count complaints monthly; **a programme with no complaints usually has an inaccessible mechanism**.
notes.67: Read the log as a model: each risk has likelihood, impact, response and owner. Severe-impact risks need a response even when unlikely, such as child abuse rated low likelihood and severe impact. Review the log **quarterly and after any incident**.
notes.69: An implementation plan sequences work in phases and fits it to the calendar: agricultural seasons, monsoon, school terms, festivals, the April to March financial year and the model code of conduct. Use the six components as a checklist. The last one, **decision points**, is what makes the plan adaptive.
notes.70: Fidelity falls as programmes grow, mostly because supervision thins. Plan the supervisor ratio, visit frequency and what supervisors check. Supervision that works observes delivery and coaches on the spot, while monthly paper reviews do not. Budget for turnover: **a one-time training budget assumes no one ever leaves.**
notes.71: A pilot tests whether the design can be delivered and whether the riskiest assumptions hold. Run it under conditions close to scale, with the staff and budget per participant you would use later. Agree before the pilot what result would make you change or stop, because **deciding afterwards invites reading every result as success**.
notes.72: Design monitoring around decisions. For each decision, list the information needed and how often. A short list of indicators that are checked and acted on beats a long dashboard nobody opens. The table pairs each decision with an indicator and a frequency. **Start from the decision, then pick the indicator.**
notes.73: Adaptive management adjusts a programme within agreed limits as monitoring shows what works. Problem-Driven Iterative Adaptation emphasises local problems, experimentation and fast feedback. The cycle on the slide is plan, do, check, act. Adaptation needs permission, so **agree in advance which changes the team can make alone**.
notes.74: Write flexibility into the grant. Negotiate outcome-level targets with flexibility on activities, a reallocation threshold, review points and a learning budget. Offer clear monitoring of key assumptions and early warning in return. The slide says funders who have seen a rigid grant fail are often open, so **ask explicitly**.
notes.75: Plan the end at the beginning. Four exit routes each carry a design requirement: government takes over, a community institution continues, the programme is time-limited by design, or a market continues. A programme meant for handover should use the department's staff and norms from the pilot. **Write the exit route into the theory of change.**
notes.77: Most programmes reach scale through the state, so an NGO programme matters mainly if it changes what government systems do. Government offers reach, permanence and mandate, and constrains with norms, procurement and transfers. The advice: **aim to change a scheme's design, guidelines or delivery practice**, which reaches further than a parallel programme.
notes.78: Study the rural employment scheme as an example of designing within a scheme. The Act guarantees 125 days, plans through gram panchayat plans, allows a 60-day pause at peak seasons and gives each state a normative allocation, with excess borne by the state. The table gives an NGO implication for each feature. **Check the current text** after 1 July 2026.
notes.79: Choose from five ways to work with government: technical support, embedded implementation, adoption of a model, contracted delivery and joint evaluation. Each needs a formal agreement, usually an MoU, setting roles, data sharing, branding and exit. **Pick the model before you negotiate**, because it shapes what you can promise.
notes.80: JEEViKA grew from a World Bank project in 42 blocks to a model for the National Rural Livelihoods Mission. It was run by an autonomous society, saturated its first blocks and expanded in phases. The open questions are about quality at national scale. **Loged-for-purpose delivery and phased expansion** are the transferable lessons.
notes.81: Separate horizontal scaling (more districts and participants) from vertical scaling (policy, budgets and law). Plan for scalability from the start using the CORRECT checklist. A design that needs rare staff, an expensive input or a charismatic leader will not scale, so **remove those dependencies early**.
notes.82: Effects shrink at scale. In Kenya, contract teachers hired by an NGO raised scores and identical teachers hired by the government produced no effect. The table pairs each cause with a design response: pilot through the scaling implementer, do political economy analysis, plan supervision. **Test in typical sites** and measure spillovers.
notes.83: Evaluate inside the government system so that results answer what happens if the state does it itself. Plan with the department, randomise at block or district level where spillovers matter, use administrative data and agree how results will be used. Ethics and data law still apply, so **involve an ethics committee**.
notes.85: Follow the worked example step by step: data first, then the problem statement, causes, scope, and stakeholders. The example is illustrative. Note how the vacancies row is placed outside scope and noted as an assumption. Each decision is written with its reason so the funder can see **what was left out and why**.
notes.86: See how three options are compared on fit with scale. Pratham-style camps are rejected for the main design because they are parallel to school, the government teacher model is chosen, and books are kept as an add-on. The team accepts lower fidelity and plans mentoring to protect it. **The choice follows the exit route.**
notes.87: Follow the example to targeting, budget and risks. Geographic targeting avoids documents, the budget is built bottom up with a safeguarding line, and the top risks pair with responses. The slide notes that a real design would attach the full budget and risk log as annexes. **Pair every risk with a response and an owner.**
notes.88: The implementation plan turns monitoring into decisions through rules agreed in advance. If sessions held fall below 60%, redesign the timetable. If mentor visits fall below one a month, renegotiate mentor time. **Without agreed rules every result is read as a reason to continue.**
notes.89: Use part one of the checklist to review your own design or a proposal you appraise. It covers problem and people, then stakeholders and evidence. Each unticked item is a question to ask the team. Pay special attention to **dated sources, marginal groups consulted and null results**.
notes.90: Use part two for intervention, targeting, plan, risk and scale. It asks for at least three options, a cash benchmark, a delivery model you would use at scale and a pilot with decision rules. The closing warning is sound: a design ticking every item can still fail, and **one ticking few has usually not been thought through**.
notes.91: Use the seven questions when you appraise someone else's design, and compare each answer with the weak form in the right-hand column. 'All poor households' is not targeting, and 'the community will take over' is not an exit. **Ask for written answers.**
notes.93: Use the table as a diagnostic of seven recurring failures: solution first, wrong cause, ignored incentives, thin dosage, pilot-only conditions, exclusion by design, no learning loop. Each has a prevention. The slide's last line is a promise: **most are visible in the design document** if someone asks the right question before the grant is signed.
notes.94: The Udaipur case is a design failure in a precise sense. Attendance rose by 15 to 29 percentage points at first, and then the enforcing administration damaged machines and excused absences. The design assumed enforcers would punish their own staff. Ask of every rule: **who enforces it, and what do they gain or lose?**
notes.95: Do not promise more than the mechanism delivers. The Hyderabad evaluation found more investment and no significant rise in average consumption, yet designs promised poverty reduction through credit alone. Monitoring counted loans and repayment, which tells you about the lender. **Promise what the evidence supports**, and measure borrowers' well-being.
notes.96: A parallel programme builds beside the state. It can show strong results while funded, and when funding ends nothing in the government system has changed. Look at the warning signs: staff paid far above government scales, separate data systems and branding that hides the department. **Work through government staff and cost at government norms.**
notes.97: Run a pre-mortem for 90 minutes before finalising the design. Imagine the programme failed, write reasons independently, pool them and check each against the log, assumptions, monitoring plan and budget. Collecting in writing first stops **senior voices setting the agenda**. Then change the design where a reason points to a fixable flaw.
notes.98: Read the ten principles in two groups: before choosing and when choosing and planning. They compress the course: problem before solution, causes checked, power mapped, evidence including nulls, mechanism understood, options compared with cash, errors designed, assumptions monitored, safeguarding budgeted, and **pilot with the system that will scale it**.
notes.99: Choose your next course by the gap. Theory of Change and Logframe build the results chain, MEL Basics the learning system, Cost Effectiveness the comparison of options. The suggested order is Theory of Change, Logframe, MEL Basics, then Cost Effectiveness, and **Safeguarding & PSEA before any work with children**.
